tip: 'Opbellen' splits, and 'op' can land far from 'bellen' at the clause end: 'bellen ... op'.
Starting a clause with 'dan' flips subject and verb, so it is 'dan zie je', not 'dan je ziet'.
Dutch drops the word for 'of' in quantities, so a glass of wine is simply 'een glas rode wijn'.
'Zich afvragen' means to wonder and needs the reflexive 'me', so it is 'ik vraag me af', not 'ik vraag af'.
For 'in order to', wrap the infinitive in 'om ... te', so 'om bij het centrum te komen' means to reach the center.
Dutch says the unit before the ten, so 55 is 'vijfenvijftig', literally five-and-fifty.
Regular verbs form the past with '-te' or '-de', so 'bedanken' becomes 'bedankte' for thanked.
Verbs of change take 'zijn', not 'hebben', in the perfect, so it is 'zijn verwelkt' for have wilted.
Dutch normally uses the plain adjective as the adverb, with no -ly ending, so 'langzaam' covers both slow and slowly.
'Te koop' is a set phrase for on the market, so 'is te koop' means is for sale, not literally to buy.
'Kortom' stands outside the sentence with a comma, so it skips inversion: 'kortom, het was', subject stays first.
Dutch names things with 'heten', not 'to be': 'hoe heet je?' literally asks how you are called.
Yes/no questions just put the verb first, with no 'do' helper: 'spreekt u Engels?' (speak you English?).
'Je' is the unstressed your as well as you: 'je weekend' means your weekend; the stressed form is 'jouw'.
In 'waar kom je vandaan?', 'vandaan' breaks off and lands at the end: 'waar ... vandaan' = where ... from.
'Kind' has an irregular plural in '-eren': one 'kind', several 'kinderen'.
'Hoe gaat het met ...?' is the set way to ask how someone is doing: 'gaat het met je familie'.
'Man' is used as an exclamation regardless of gender in casual Dutch.
'Praten' takes 'over' for the topic: 'praat over haar werk' = talks about her work.
'Deze' is the 'this' for de-words: 'de stoel' becomes 'deze stoel'.
After a number, measure nouns stay singular: 'twee uur' = two hours, not 'twee uren'.
'Daarvoor' fuses 'daar' plus 'voor' to mean before that; Dutch builds these daar-words instead of 'voor dat'.
De-words take '-e' on the adjective even after 'een': 'de wijnkaart', so 'een mooie wijnkaart'.
Start with a time word and the verb still comes second, before the subject: 'gisteren heb ik'.
Days of the week take 'op': 'op zaterdag' = on Saturday.
A helper verb like 'moet' pushes the other verb to the end as an infinitive: 'moet je stil zijn'.
'Ondanks' is a preposition and takes a noun: 'ondanks de regen'. For a full clause use 'hoewel' instead.
In an indirect question the verb goes to the very end: 'hoe oud je bent', not 'hoe oud bent je'.
Verbs of motion to a destination take 'zijn', not 'hebben', in the perfect: 'is ... aangekomen' = has arrived.
In the perfect, a separable verb tucks '-ge-' inside: 'thuiskomen' becomes 'thuisgekomen'.
